title: Add a New Outlet
summary: Add a new tamper-resistant outlet by running cable from an existing outlet on a suitable circuit to an old-work box, with a permit, the right wire size and the right protection for the room.
safety: Most areas require a permit and inspection for new wiring. Turn the breaker off and prove every wire dead with a tested non-contact tester before touching anything. Wire size must match the breaker. Never extend kitchen countertop, bathroom, laundry or dedicated circuits. Check for pipes and wires before cutting or drilling.
pro: the source has no ground, you find aluminum wire, cloth insulation or scorch marks, the circuit is already loaded or trips, the panel is full or you need a new circuit, the wire is smaller than the breaker requires, or your area doesn't let homeowners pull an electrical permit.

steps.t: Stop: don't extend this circuit
steps.idea: Kitchen countertop, bathroom and laundry outlets are on circuits that must not feed other outlets.
steps.b:
1. Don't add outlets to kitchen countertop, bathroom or laundry circuits, or to any dedicated circuit (fridge, microwave, dishwasher, furnace, sump pump).
  2. These rooms usually need their own new circuits from the panel, with GFCI (and often AFCI) protection.
  3. Call a licensed electrician to quote a new circuit.
  4. Want an outlet in another room instead? Change your answer on the Start tab.
steps.stop: Adding outlets to these circuits overloads them and is not allowed in most codes. This is a job for an electrician.

steps.t: Call your building department
steps.idea: Most areas require a permit and inspection for any new wiring, even one outlet.
steps.b:
1. Call or check the website of your city or county building department.
  2. Ask: "Do I need a permit to add one outlet by extending a circuit? Can a homeowner pull it?"
  3. Ask which protection they require in this room: AFCI (arc-fault) and/or GFCI (ground-fault), and whether an AFCI breaker or an AFCI outlet is accepted.
  4. Ask when they want to inspect: before you close any walls (rough-in), at the end (final), or both.
  5. Write down the answers and apply for the permit.
faq: What if I skip the permit?
Unpermitted wiring can cause problems with insurance claims and home sales, and nobody checks your work. Pull the permit.
They say only licensed electricians can pull permits.
Then hire one. Some will let you do the prep (cutting, fishing) and do the connections themselves.

steps.t: Map the circuit and check its load
steps.idea: Find everything on the breaker and make sure it has room for more.
steps.b:
1. Plug a lamp or radio into the outlet you plan to use as the source. Turn off breakers one at a time until it goes off.
  2. Leave that breaker off. Walk the house: list every outlet and light that is now dead (plug the tester into each outlet).
  3. Is anything on the list in a kitchen countertop, bathroom or laundry? Or a fridge, microwave, space heater, window AC or other big load? Pick a different circuit.
  4. Does this breaker ever trip? Pick a different circuit.
  5. As a rule of thumb, keep the steady load under about 80% of the breaker: about 12 A on a 15 A breaker, 16 A on a 20 A breaker.
  6. Write the breaker number down.
steps.stop: If the circuit already trips, feeds a kitchen counter, bathroom or laundry, or is a dedicated circuit, don't extend it.
faq: How do I know what something draws?
Look at the label on the plug or the back of the appliance: amps, or watts divided by 120.

steps.t: Choose a source outlet
steps.idea: Power for the new outlet comes from an existing outlet with a neutral and a ground.
steps.b:
1. Pick an outlet on the circuit you checked, as close as possible to where the new one goes, ideally on the same wall.
  2. It must be always-on: not controlled by a wall switch.
  3. It should have a ground: the plug-in tester shows "correct", not "open ground".
  4. Don't use a switch box: many have no neutral wire.
  5. It can be at the end of the run (one cable) or in the middle (two cables). You will check the box size in the parts step.
faq: Can I use a GFCI outlet as the source?
Yes. If you connect the new cable to its LOAD terminals, the GFCI protects the new outlet too. If unsure, connect it with pigtails to LINE and protect the new outlet separately.
The tester says open ground.
No ground at the source. Don't extend from it. Ask an electrician.

steps.t: Match the cable to the breaker
steps.idea: The new wire must be at least as thick as the breaker requires, and match the existing wire.
steps.b:
1. Read the amp number on the breaker handle: 15 or 20.
  2. 15 A breaker: 14 AWG wire (14/2 with ground NM-B, often white sheath).
  3. 20 A breaker: 12 AWG wire (12/2 with ground NM-B, often yellow sheath).
  4. When you open the source box, read the print on its cable sheath and make sure it matches.
  5. Don't trust sheath color alone. The printing is what counts.
steps.stop: If you find 14 AWG wire on a 20 A breaker, the existing circuit is unsafe. Stop and have an electrician fix it.

steps.t: Plan the route and find the studs
steps.idea: Choose a path that misses studs' faces, pipes, ducts and fire blocking.
steps.b:
1. Mark the studs between the source and the new spot with the stud finder. Light pencil marks.
  2. Put the new box between two studs, at the same height as the other outlets (measure floor to bottom of the source box).
  3. Check the other side of the wall and the floor below (basement) for pipes, drains, ducts or other cables in the same bays.
  4. Avoid exterior walls if you can: insulation makes fishing much harder.
  5. Fewer studs = easier. Same stud bay is easiest, one or two studs over is fine. Your plan crosses about {{c.studs}}. More than 3 or 4, or a fire block in the way? Consider opening the wall.
faq: What is fire blocking?

Horizontal blocks of wood between studs, common in older homes and taller walls. A flex bit can drill through, but you can't see it. Knock lightly along the wall: a solid sound mid-wall can be blocking.
Can I go through the basement instead?
Often yes: drill up through the bottom plate of each wall bay. It's a good route if you have an open basement ceiling, but it uses more cable and more drilling. The same rules apply.

steps.t: Buy parts and check box size
steps.idea: Every box has a maximum number of wires. Too many and the connections overheat.
steps.b:
1. Read the Start tab: your source box needs at least {{c.srcVol}} cu in after the new cable is added. The new box needs at least {{c.newVol}} cu in.
  2. When you open the source box, find its volume stamped inside. If it's smaller than {{c.srcVol}} cu in, choose another source or plan a bigger box.
  3. Buy an old-work (remodel) box with wings or ears, 1-gang, at least {{c.newVol}} cu in. About 20 cu in gives room to work.
  4. Buy cable: {{c.cable}} ft needed, so a {{c.roll}} ft roll of {{a.amps==='20'?'12/2':'14/2'}} NM-B with ground.
  5. Buy the outlet for the room ({{a.room==='garage'?'GFCI':'tamper-resistant, plus AFCI protection as your inspector requires'}}).
faq: The source box has no volume stamped on it.
Common old metal 1-gang boxes are small, often under 18 cu in. Measure it, or assume it's too small and pick a source with more room.

steps.t: Turn off the breaker and prove it dead
steps.idea: Kill the circuit at the panel and test before you touch anything.
steps.b:
1. Turn off the breaker you wrote down. Tape over it: "Working on outlet. Don't touch."
  2. Test your non-contact tester on a known live outlet. It must beep.
  3. Plug the plug-in tester into both halves of the source outlet: no lights.
  4. Hold the pen at the short slot of each half: silence.
  5. Test the pen on the live outlet again.
steps.stop: If anything beeps or lights, stop and find the right breaker.

steps.t: Open the source box and inspect it
steps.idea: Look before you commit: the wiring and box must be good enough to extend.
steps.b:
1. Remove the plate and the two outlet mounting screws. Pull the outlet straight out.
  2. Hold the tester to every wire in the box. Silence everywhere.
  3. Photograph the wiring.
  4. Count cables and wires. Read the volume stamped in the box and the print on the cable sheath (14 or 12 AWG).
  5. Check for a bare ground wire connected to the outlet (and to the box if metal).
  6. Plastic box nailed to a stud, or metal box? Note it for the next steps.
steps.stop: Stop and call an electrician if you see: no ground wire, aluminum (dull silver) wire, cloth or crumbling insulation, scorch marks, wire smaller than the breaker needs, or a box too small for one more cable.

steps.t: Mark and cut the new box hole
steps.idea: A clean, accurate hole is what lets the old-work box clamp tight.
steps.b:
1. Hold the new box's face (not the ears) to the wall between studs, at the same height as the source box. Level it and trace around it.
  2. Recheck with the stud finder that no stud is under the outline.
  3. Cut or drill a small test hole in the middle of the outline. Shine a light in and feel around with a bent wire for pipes, cables and blocking.
  4. All clear? Cut on the line with the jab saw. Push gently; don't punch through hard (there may be wires behind).
  5. Test-fit the box. It should slide in snug with the ears flat on the wall. Trim only where it binds.
faq: I cut the hole too big.
The ears won't hold. Patch and recut a little to the side, or use a box with bigger ears plus a box-support bracket (madison strap).
There's a stud right there.
Move over to the next bay. That's why you test first.

steps.t: Open a knockout in the source box
steps.idea: The new cable needs a way into the existing box.
steps.b:
1. Plastic box: find a knockout tab on the side facing the new outlet (or top/bottom). Push it in with a flat screwdriver and break it off cleanly. Some tabs just flex: leave those, they hold the cable.
  2. Metal box: pry out a round knockout and plan to install a cable clamp (NM connector) in it. Many metal boxes have built-in clamps instead.
  3. Hold the existing wires aside so you don't damage their insulation.
  4. Feel inside the wall through the knockout: you should be able to reach the wall cavity.
faq: There's no knockout I can use.
Some boxes are tight against a stud. An electrician can replace the source box with a larger old-work box, which also solves box fill.

steps.t: Drill through the studs with a flex bit
steps.idea: Bore a path through each stud at outlet height without opening the wall.
steps.b:
1. Feed the flex bit through the new box hole and bend it toward the source.
  2. Rest the tip against the side of the first stud at mid-depth (center of the stud).
  3. Drill slowly, keeping the bit straight and level. Let the bit do the work.
  4. Continue to the next stud: reach through the hole you just made, or from the source box side.
  5. Many flex bits have a hole in the tip. Once through the last stud, clip the cable to it and pull it back (or use the fish tape next).
  6. Never drill blind near the 1-1/4" face zone: if you can't keep the bit centered, open the wall at that stud.
steps.stop: If the bit hits metal, stop at once and look: it may be a pipe, nail plate or another cable.
faq: Do I need nail plates here?
If every hole is at mid-depth (more than 1-1/4" from both faces), no. If you're unsure, open a small square of drywall at that stud, add a plate, and patch it.

steps.t: Open the wall and drill the studs
steps.idea: With a strip of drywall removed you can see and drill every stud cleanly.
steps.b:
1. Score a 6" tall strip of drywall from the source box to the new box at outlet height. Cut the vertical edges along stud centers so the patch has backing.
  2. Remove the strip carefully and keep it for patching.
  3. Drill a 3/4" hole through the center of each stud, at the same height.
  4. Any hole closer than 1-1/4" to the stud face: nail a steel nail plate over it.
  5. Leave the wall open until your inspector says it can be closed.

steps.t: Fish the cable
steps.idea: Pull the new cable from the new box hole to the source box.
steps.b:
1. Push the fish tape from the source box knockout (or the source bay) through the stud holes to the new box hole.
  2. Strip 3" of sheath off the cable end. Hook the bare wires through the tape's hook and fold them back.
  3. Wrap electrical tape over the joint, smooth and tapered.
  4. Have a helper feed the cable at the new box while you pull at the source. Pull steady; don't yank against sharp edges.
  5. Pull until about 12" of cable sticks out of the source box. Leave 12" out of the new box hole too, then cut it off the roll.
  6. Cables fished inside a finished wall don't need staples.
faq: The fish tape won't reach the source box.
Fish to the source bay first, then push a stiff wire or a short fish tape out through the knockout from inside the box and hook the cable in.
The cable is stuck.
Pull it back a bit and try again. Kinks and big tape joints are the usual cause.

steps.t: Strip the cable ends
steps.idea: Remove the outer sheath without nicking the wires inside.
steps.b:
1. At each end, measure where the cable will enter the box. Mark 1/4" inside that point.
  2. Slide the cable ripper on from the end and slit the sheath back to your mark. Peel it back and cut it off.
  3. Cut away the paper wrap.
  4. You want at least 6" of free wire from where the sheath ends, and at least 3" sticking past the box face. Cut the rest off.
  5. Check the insulated wires for nicks. Nicked? Cut back and redo.

steps.t: Install the old-work box
steps.idea: Feed the cable in first, then set the box so it clamps the drywall.
steps.b:
1. Push the new cable through one of the box's cable entries (clamp tab) from the back, so 1/4" of sheath shows inside.
  2. Slide the box into the hole, ears flat on the wall, cable following.
  3. Tighten the wing screws a little at a time, alternating top and bottom.
  4. Stop when the box is snug and doesn't wiggle. Overtightening crushes the drywall.
  5. Check: sheath 1/4" inside, cable not pinched by the wings.
faq: The box spins or the wings miss.
The hole is too big or the drywall crumbled. Use a box-support bracket or ask for help.

steps.t: Connect at the source with pigtails
steps.idea: Join the new cable to the existing wires so power continues to the new outlet.
steps.b:
1. Remove the wires from the source outlet. If it had wires on two pairs of screws, those cables go into the bundles too.
  2. Cut three 6" pigtails from leftover cable: black, white, bare.
  3. Blacks: existing black(s) + new black + black pigtail under one wire nut. Twist clockwise until tight.
  4. Whites: same, with the white pigtail. Grounds: same, with the bare pigtail (metal box: add a second ground pigtail to the box's green screw).
  5. Tug every wire. None may pull out.
  6. Pigtails to the outlet: bare to green, white to silver, black to brass, clockwise. Use a new TR outlet if the old one is worn.
steps.stop: Never connect black to white. If the source has a red wire or the outlet's tab between the brass screws is broken off, it's split or switched: stop and ask an electrician.
faq: Can I use the second set of screws instead?
Pigtails are the better practice and are required on some multiwire circuits. Use them.

steps.t: Wire the new outlet
steps.idea: Ground to green, white to silver, black to brass.
steps.b:
1. Strip 3/4" off each insulated wire.
  2. Ground: bare wire clockwise around the green screw. Tighten.
  3. {{a.room==='garage'?'GFCI: white to the LINE silver terminal, black to the LINE brass terminal. Leave the LOAD terminals taped.':'Neutral: white clockwise around a silver screw. Tighten firmly.'}}
  4. {{a.room==='garage'?'Tighten the clamp screws firmly.':'Hot: black clockwise around a brass screw. Tighten firmly.'}}
  5. Tug each wire. Tighten any unused screws.
faq: Where does AFCI protection go?

It depends on what your inspector accepts: an AFCI breaker in the panel protects the whole circuit; an AFCI (or dual-function) outlet at the first outlet on the circuit protects everything after it. Follow the device instructions.

steps.t: Fold the wires and mount both outlets
steps.idea: Tuck the wires neatly so nothing loosens or gets pinched.
steps.b:
1. Fold the wires behind each outlet in an accordion shape. Wire nuts toward the back of the box.
  2. Push each outlet straight in and screw it to the box until snug and straight.
  3. Attach the cover plates.

steps.t: Power on and test both outlets
steps.idea: Prove the old outlet still works and the new one is wired correctly.
steps.b:
1. Remove the tape and turn the breaker on.
  2. Plug the tester into both halves of the source outlet: "correct".
  3. Plug it into both halves of the new outlet: "correct".
  4. {{a.room==='garage'?'Press TEST on the GFCI: power goes off. Press RESET: power returns.':'If you added an AFCI device, press its TEST button: power goes off. Reset it.'}}
  5. Check that the other outlets downstream of the source still work.
faq: The tester shows open neutral or no power.
A wire nut at the source isn't gripping. Breaker off, prove dead, redo that connection.
The breaker trips right away.
A hot is touching ground or neutral somewhere. Breaker off and check both boxes for pinched or swapped wires.

steps.t: Get it inspected
steps.idea: An inspector checks the work before it's hidden for good.
steps.b:
1. Schedule the inspection your building department asked for.
  2. {{a.route==='open'?'Leave the wall open until the inspector signs off.':'Leave the plates off if the inspector wants to see the connections.'}}
  3. Have the box volume, cable type and breaker size ready to show.
  4. Fix anything on the correction list, then reschedule.

steps.t: Patch the wall
steps.idea: Close the access strip once the inspector approves.
steps.b:
1. Screw the saved drywall strip back to the studs (add wood backing strips if an edge has no stud).
  2. Tape the seams with mesh tape.
  3. Spread a thin coat of joint compound. Let it dry fully (premixed: overnight; quick-set: per the bag).
  4. Add 1–2 more thin, wider coats, drying between.
  5. Sand smooth, prime and paint.

days.t: Plan, check the circuit, get the permit

testHelp.b:
1. Turn it on (some have a button you hold).
  2. Touch the tip to the short slot of an outlet you know is live. It should beep or flash.
  3. Now hold it at the outlet or wire you're testing. Silence means no voltage detected.
  4. Test it on the live outlet again afterward. A dead battery gives a false "safe".

hookHelp.b:
1. Strip 3/4" of insulation using the right gauge hole.
  2. Grip the very end with needle-nose pliers and roll it into a U.
  3. Hook it around the screw so the open end points clockwise.
  4. Squeeze the hook closed, then tighten the screw firmly.

studHelp.b:
1. Hold it flat on the wall and press the button before you move it (it calibrates on a hollow spot).
  2. Slide slowly sideways. Mark where it lights up from each direction; the stud is between the marks.
  3. Studs are usually 16" apart. Confirm with a tiny nail hole where the plate will cover it.

fishHelp.t: Use a fish tape or glow rods
fishHelp.b:
1. Unreel only what you need and keep the reel close to the opening.
  2. Push gently and twist slightly to get past obstacles. Don't force it.
  3. Glow rods are stiff and snap together: better for straight pushes across a bay.
  4. Pull the cable steadily, with a helper feeding it so it doesn't kink.

route.svg: <text x="10" y="14" class="k">Plan the route</text><rect x="20" y="40" width="6" height="146" class="w"/><rect x="84" y="40" width="6" height="146" class="w"/><rect x="148" y="40" width="6" height="146" class="w"/><rect x="212" y="40" width="6" height="146" class="w"/><rect x="276" y="40" width="6" height="146" class="w"/><line x1="10" y1="186" x2="310" y2="186" class="o" style="stroke-width:2"/><rect x="90" y="80" width="58" height="6" class="w"/><text x="92" y="74">fire block</text><rect x="258" y="40" width="6" height="146" class="wt"/><text x="220" y="60" class="wa">pipe:</text><text x="220" y="72">avoid</text><line x1="58" y1="143" x2="172" y2="143" class="a" style="stroke-width:3"/><circle cx="87" cy="143" r="3.5" class="bk"/><circle cx="151" cy="143" r="3.5" class="bk"/><rect x="42" y="130" width="16" height="26" rx="2" class="bk"/><rect x="172" y="130" width="16" height="26" rx="2" class="mos"/><text x="30" y="124">source</text><text x="160" y="124" class="ac">new</text><text x="84" y="200">drill studs at outlet height</text>
route.cap: Studs are usually 16" apart. Run the cable straight across at outlet height, between pipes and under any fire blocking.

nailplate.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Holes in the middle of the stud</text><rect x="10" y="36" width="300" height="8" class="b"/><rect x="10" y="149" width="300" height="8" class="b"/><rect x="50" y="44" width="45" height="105" class="w"/><rect x="210" y="44" width="45" height="105" class="w"/><line x1="50" y1="81" x2="95" y2="81" class="o d"/><line x1="210" y1="81" x2="255" y2="81" class="o d"/><line x1="20" y1="96" x2="125" y2="96" class="a" style="stroke-width:3"/><circle cx="72" cy="96" r="7" class="o" fill="none"/><line x1="180" y1="62" x2="285" y2="62" class="a" style="stroke-width:3"/><circle cx="232" cy="62" r="7" class="o" fill="none"/><rect x="204" y="40" width="57" height="5" class="inkf"/><text x="100" y="84">1-1/4"</text><text x="260" y="84">1-1/4"</text><text x="10" y="180" class="gd">centered: OK</text><text x="150" y="180" class="wa">near the face: nail plate</text>
nailplate.title: Top view of a stud
nailplate.cap: If a hole is closer than 1-1/4" to the face of the stud, nail a steel plate over it so drywall screws can't hit the cable.

flexbit.svg: <text x="10" y="14" class="k">Drill through the box hole</text><rect x="10" y="60" width="90" height="6" class="b"/><rect x="130" y="60" width="180" height="6" class="b"/><rect x="40" y="66" width="15" height="35" class="w"/><rect x="200" y="66" width="15" height="35" class="w"/><rect x="104" y="22" width="28" height="16" rx="3" class="y"/><path d="M118 38 L116 66 Q112 86 58 86" class="o" fill="none" stroke-dasharray="130" style="stroke-width:3"><animate attributeName="stroke-dashoffset" values="130;0;0" keyTimes="0;0.7;1" dur="3s" repeatCount="indefinite"/></path><text x="140" y="34" class="k">drill + long flex bit</text><text x="220" y="54">drywall</text><text x="40" y="114">stud</text><text x="10" y="134">Feed the bit in through the new box hole,</text><text x="10" y="146">bend it toward the stud and drill at</text><text x="10" y="158">mid-depth, level with the outlets.</text>
flexbit.title: Drill with a flex bit
flexbit.cap: A flex bit (installer bit) bends inside the wall so you can reach the next stud without opening the drywall.

fish.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Hook the cable to the fish tape</text><line x1="10" y1="70" x2="150" y2="70" class="o" style="stroke-width:2.5"/><rect x="170" y="64" width="140" height="12" rx="6" class="bk"/><path d="M170 67 C150 62 150 78 170 73" class="o" fill="none" style="stroke-width:2"/><rect x="140" y="61" width="44" height="18" rx="4" class="y"/><text x="10" y="56" class="k">fish tape</text><text x="250" y="56" class="k">cable</text><text x="162" y="98" class="ac" text-anchor="middle">taped smooth</text><text x="10" y="126">Bend the bare wires through the hook,</text><text x="10" y="138">then wrap tape so nothing can snag.</text>
fish.cap: A bulky joint snags on stud holes. Strip back only what you need and taper the tape wrap.

cuthole.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Trace and cut the box hole</text><line x1="30" y1="30" x2="30" y2="150" class="o d"/><line x1="230" y1="30" x2="230" y2="150" class="o d"/><rect x="88" y="44" width="64" height="8" rx="2" class="y"/><circle cx="120" cy="48" r="3" class="o" fill="none"/><rect x="100" y="60" width="40" height="64" class="a" fill="none" style="stroke-width:2"/><circle cx="120" cy="92" r="5" class="bk"/><text x="34" y="30">stud</text><text x="234" y="140">stud</text><text x="88" y="40" class="k">level</text><text x="240" y="70" class="k">trace the</text><text x="240" y="82">box outline</text><text x="240" y="110" class="k">small test</text><text x="240" y="122">hole first</text><line x1="126" y1="92" x2="236" y2="112" class="o d"/><text x="10" y="166">Between studs, same height as the other</text><text x="10" y="178">outlets. Cut on the line with a drywall saw.</text>
cuthole.cap: Look and feel through the test hole for pipes, wires, studs and blocking before you cut the full outline.

strip.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Strip the cable sheathing</text><rect x="120" y="30" width="90" height="110" rx="3" class="bk"/><line x1="140" y1="132" x2="174" y2="132" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><rect x="150" y="124" width="16" height="46" class="b"/><path d="M153 124 C150 90 140 60 140 34" class="o" fill="none" style="stroke-width:3"/><path d="M158 124 C158 90 158 60 158 34" class="o" fill="none" style="stroke-width:1.5"/><path d="M163 124 C166 90 176 60 176 34" class="o" fill="none" style="stroke-width:3"/><line x1="216" y1="34" x2="216" y2="124" class="a" style="stroke-width:2"/><text x="222" y="56" class="k">6" free wire</text><text x="222" y="68">at least 3"</text><text x="222" y="80">past the face</text><text x="222" y="120" class="k">1/4" of sheath</text><text x="222" y="132">past the clamp</text><text x="10" y="96">Cable ripper:</text><text x="10" y="108">slit, peel back,</text><text x="10" y="120">cut it off.</text>
strip.cap: The sheath must enter the box about 1/4" past the clamp so no bare insulated wire sits in the clamp.

oldwork.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Old-work box: wings clamp behind</text><rect x="150" y="30" width="10" height="114" class="b"/><rect x="160" y="62" width="60" height="66" class="bk"/><rect x="144" y="56" width="6" height="78" class="bk"/><line x1="150" y1="72" x2="160" y2="72" class="o"/><line x1="150" y1="118" x2="160" y2="118" class="o"/><g><rect x="160" y="46" width="4" height="16" class="inkf"/><animateTransform attributeName="transform" type="rotate" values="90 162 62;90 162 62;0 162 62;0 162 62" keyTimes="0;0.3;0.7;1" dur="3s" repeatCount="indefinite"/></g><g><rect x="160" y="128" width="4" height="16" class="inkf"/><animateTransform attributeName="transform" type="rotate" values="-90 162 128;-90 162 128;0 162 128;0 162 128" keyTimes="0;0.3;0.7;1" dur="3s" repeatCount="indefinite"/></g><rect x="40" y="91" width="96" height="8" rx="3" class="y"/><text x="10" y="44" class="k">room side</text><text x="230" y="44" class="k">inside wall</text><text x="40" y="84">screwdriver</text><text x="96" y="138">drywall</text><text x="10" y="160">Tighten the screws: the wings swing out</text><text x="10" y="172">and clamp the drywall from behind.</text>
oldwork.title: Set an old-work box
oldwork.cap: Snug, not tight: overtightening crushes the drywall and the box goes loose.

pigtail.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">At the source: pigtail</text><line x1="10" y1="60" x2="120" y2="80" class="o" style="stroke-width:5"/><line x1="10" y1="104" x2="120" y2="86" class="a" style="stroke-width:5"/><line x1="140" y1="83" x2="236" y2="83" class="o" style="stroke-width:5"/><path d="M118 70 h26 l6 13 l-6 13 h-26z" class="y"/><circle cx="252" cy="83" r="12" class="y"/><line x1="244" y1="83" x2="260" y2="83" class="o"/><text x="10" y="52">existing cable</text><text x="10" y="124" class="ac">NEW cable</text><text x="132" y="116" class="k" text-anchor="middle">wire nut</text><text x="170" y="74" class="ac">6" pigtail</text><text x="270" y="87">outlet</text><text x="10" y="150">Blacks + pigtail. Whites + pigtail.</text><text x="10" y="162">Grounds + pigtail. Tug every wire.</text>
pigtail.cap: Pigtails keep one wire per screw and keep power flowing through even if the outlet fails.

boxfill.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Count what is in the box</text><text x="10" y="38">Each hot or neutral wire</text><text x="310" y="38" class="k" text-anchor="end">1 each</text><text x="10" y="52">All grounds together</text><text x="310" y="52" class="k" text-anchor="end">1</text><text x="10" y="66">The outlet (device)</text><text x="310" y="66" class="k" text-anchor="end">2</text><text x="10" y="80">Internal cable clamps</text><text x="310" y="80" class="k" text-anchor="end">1</text><text x="10" y="94">Wires that never leave</text><text x="310" y="94" class="k" text-anchor="end">0</text><text x="10" y="108">the box (pigtails)</text><line x1="10" y1="120" x2="310" y2="120" class="o"/><text x="10" y="136" class="k">Total x 2.0 cu in (14 AWG)</text><text x="10" y="150" class="k">Total x 2.25 cu in (12 AWG)</text><text x="10" y="170">Box must be at least that. Volume is</text><text x="10" y="182">stamped inside, e.g. "18 CU IN".</text>
boxfill.cap: The Start tab does this math for your source box and new box. Too small? Pick another source or a bigger box.

anatomy.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Know the screws</text><rect x="110" y="24" width="100" height="156" rx="14" class="bk"/><rect x="138" y="40" width="6" height="22" rx="1" class="inkf"/><rect x="176" y="43" width="6" height="16" rx="1" class="inkf"/><path d="M154 74 a6 6 0 0 1 12 0 v6 h-12z" class="inkf"/><rect x="138" y="112" width="6" height="22" rx="1" class="inkf"/><rect x="176" y="115" width="6" height="16" rx="1" class="inkf"/><path d="M154 146 a6 6 0 0 1 12 0 v6 h-12z" class="inkf"/><circle cx="216" cy="66" r="7" class="y"/><line x1="211" y1="66" x2="221" y2="66" class="o"/><circle cx="104" cy="66" r="7" class="bk"/><line x1="99" y1="66" x2="109" y2="66" class="o"/><circle cx="216" cy="138" r="7" class="y"/><line x1="211" y1="138" x2="221" y2="138" class="o"/><circle cx="104" cy="138" r="7" class="bk"/><line x1="99" y1="138" x2="109" y2="138" class="o"/><circle cx="160" cy="186" r="7" class="goodf"/><text x="230" y="62" class="k">brass screw</text><text x="230" y="74">HOT · black</text><text x="90" y="62" class="k" text-anchor="end">silver screw</text><text x="90" y="74" text-anchor="end">NEUTRAL · white</text><text x="176" y="190" class="gd">green = GROUND</text><text x="176" y="201">bare wire</text>
anatomy.cap: Black to brass, white to silver, bare copper to green. Wrap each wire clockwise under its screw.

testers.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Two testers, two jobs</text><rect x="20" y="40" width="80" height="110" rx="10" class="bk"/><rect x="44" y="70" width="5" height="18" class="inkf"/><rect x="70" y="72" width="5" height="14" class="inkf"/><g transform="rotate(-25 110 70)"><rect x="96" y="34" width="20" height="90" rx="8" class="y"/><rect x="100" y="28" width="12" height="10" class="badf"/></g><path d="M126 44 q8 -8 0 -16 M134 48 q12 -12 0 -24" class="bad"/><text x="20" y="166" class="k">Non-contact pen</text><text x="20" y="178">beeps near a live wire</text><rect x="190" y="40" width="90" height="70" rx="8" class="bk"/><circle cx="214" cy="62" r="7" class="y"/><circle cx="235" cy="62" r="7" class="y"/><circle cx="256" cy="62" r="7" class="bk"/><rect x="210" y="110" width="6" height="18" class="inkf"/><rect x="254" y="110" width="6" height="18" class="inkf"/><rect x="232" y="114" width="6" height="16" class="inkf"/><text x="190" y="166" class="k">Plug-in tester</text><text x="190" y="178">checks wiring after</text>
testers.cap: Always test the pen on an outlet you know is live first, so you know it works.

glossary: The existing outlet you take power from.
A box with wings or ears that clamps to existing drywall. Also called a remodel box.
Non-metallic sheathed cable (often called Romex). "14/2 W/G" = two 14-gauge wires plus a ground.
Wire gauge. Smaller number = thicker wire: 12 AWG is thicker than 14 AWG.
The limit on how many wires a box can hold, based on its volume.
A short wire joined to the house wires with a wire nut, so only one wire goes to the outlet screw.
Arc-fault circuit interrupter: shuts off power when it detects arcing that can start a fire.
Ground-fault circuit interrupter: shuts off power if current leaks, for example through a person.
Tamper-resistant: outlets with shutters that keep kids from pushing things in.
A long, bendable drill bit for drilling inside closed walls.
A steel plate over a stud hole that stops screws and nails from hitting the cable.
Horizontal wood blocks between studs that slow fire spread.
